title: Wren and the Lost Lamb
markdown:
Wren’s den smelled of warm earth and sleep. That was how he liked it. He was a wolf pup, fur the soft grey of twilight, eyes like two amber marbles. He loved watching his mother doze by the fire, her snores a far thunder. Pine needles clung to her coat. That smell meant safe.

He was still quite small. When the wind howled at the entrance, he felt like a dry leaf. His whiskers quivered even on happy days.

Clover, a sheepdog the colour of sun-bleached straw, was his best friend. Her tail never stopped. She herded dandelion fluff into neat white piles and chased leaves into swirls. She did not worry. Her paws were always ready.

One afternoon Wren was practising his quietest pounce near the woods when he heard a sound: a tiny heartbroken bleat, a little bell with a crack in it.

“Oh, dear,” he whispered. His ears tipped forward.

He padded on. Clover trotted beside him, tail thump-thumping the tall grass. They rounded a clump of ferns. There, huddled by the reeds, was a lamb. Fleece like fresh cream. Eyes wide and wet. Soft hiccupping bleats.

“Mama?” she whimpered. “Where’s Mama?”

“You’re lost, little one,” Clover said. “Don’t worry. We’ll help you find her.”

The lamb sniffled. “I’m Lily. I followed a butterfly with wings like stained glass, and now I can’t find my flock. They were right here.”

Wren looked at Lily, then at the sky, which was turning deep purple. The Moon Meadow lay between them and the distant hills where the sheep slept: a wide shimmer of grass. The flock’s bleating sounded very far.

If they did not hurry, fog would roll in from the Whispering River. Lily would spend the night in the cold dark, and her mama would be sad.

Wren gulped. The meadow was beautiful and big and not theirs. Sometimes the grass grew taller than he was. “We have to go,” he said, trying to sound braver than his paws. He wanted the den. He stood still a moment, small and grey, then stepped.

“Right then!” Clover’s tail made a determined wag. “Lily, you walk between us. Wren, keep your nose on the bleats. I’ll watch the path.”

They stepped into silver grass that whispered as they walked. Specks of light sat on the blades as if the moon had shaken flour. Lily, a puff of white, trotted between them. Once she stopped to nose a flower; Clover herded her onward with a gentle shoulder, the way she herded fluff, only kinder.

“It’s so different,” Wren said, voice thin. He sniffed and found only the sweet damp of moon-kissed flowers. No den-smoke. No pine. His ears worked overtime. A night bird called once and was gone. The meadow seemed to go on in every direction, a silver plate with no rim.

A rustle. Sharp. Quick. A shadowy shape moved behind a clump of moon-dandelions. Wren froze. His heart drummed. His paws felt like stones. Lily pressed into Clover’s warm side.

“Just the wind,” Clover said, nudging him. “Or a field mouse. Keep your eyes on the prize.”

He filled his lungs with cool misty air. One wobbly step. Another. He held the faint bleating like a thread. Clover did not laugh at the wobble. She only kept the path, nose down, tail a metronome.

They pushed on. The moon climbed. Silver and indigo. Once the bleats faded and Wren’s stomach dropped; then the wind turned and the thread came back, a little louder, a little nearer. Dew soaked his paws. Lily’s fleece gathered tiny stars. Then they saw them: a flock huddled like a woolly cloud, looking confused, shifting, calling for a fence that was not there.

“We found them!” Lily cried, and scampered.

But where was the shepherd? As if called by the question, a soft grey fog crept across the meadow and swallowed the moonlight. The sheep bleated louder. Panic ran through them like a wave.

“Oh, bother,” Clover muttered. Her ears drooped. “If we don’t get them to the fence, they might wander into the river.”

She looked at Wren. “I need to find the shepherd. I know the way to his hut. You stay with Lily. Keep the flock together. Don’t let them scatter.”

Wren’s eyes went wide. Alone. Sheep. Fog. A tremor ran from his paws to the tip of his tail. He could have run after Clover. Lily looked so scared. The mist kissed his nose, cold and strange. The flock made a worried chorus.

He stood as tall as he could and let out a small clear bark. Then another, a little louder. He walked among the sheep, nudging them with his nose when one drifted toward the thicker white. He kept Lily close. Her bleats were a comfort by his ear. A ewe stamped; he stamped back, tiny and serious, and she stayed. The fog made every sheep look like every other sheep. He counted by warmth, by the way Lily’s cream stood out. Something warm and small lit in his chest, like an ember that had decided to stay. He did not feel large. He felt busy, which was better.

Just when the worry felt too big, a familiar scent came through the fog: the warm, slightly smoky smell of the shepherd’s pipe. Then a hearty voice.

“Clover! You found them! Oh, thank goodness!”

Clover burst from the mist, tail in a wild wag, and behind her the shepherd. He scooped Lily up.

“Little one! You gave us a scare.” Then he saw Wren, standing near the flock. “And a wolf pup keeping them together. Remarkable.”

Clover trotted over, tail furious. “You did it, Wren.”

The moonlight, which had felt like a lonely lamp, now felt like a blanket. Wren nudged Lily. Her bleat was a happy sigh. He nudged Clover. His own tail made a small content wag. He looked at the moon, then at the path home, and did not feel like a leaf.
